title: Bēowulf
titleEn: Beowulf — Fitt XXIII: The Giant’s Sword (lines 1557–1650)
source: Fr. Klaeber, Beowulf and the Fight at Finnsburg, 1st edition (Boston: D. C. Heath & Co., 1922), pp. 58–62, lines 1557–1650 (fitt XXIII). Text follows Klaeber's printing exactly — þ, ð, æ, vowel-length macrons, a circumflex for contracted vowels (Klaeber prints one mark over the pair of vowels; we place it on the second), [brackets] for letters or words added by emendation, (parentheses) for conjectural restoration of fire-damaged letters, and Klaeber's rows of dots where words are lost. A dot under a vowel (dōgọra) is Klaeber's sign that the vowel does not count in the metre. Transcribed from the page images of the archive.org scan, every page read twice. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed late West Saxon, c. 1000, following Campbell's Old English Grammar — and the recorded reading follows it, within stated limits. No synthetic voice for Old English exists, so the reading is produced by an American English neural voice under per-word phonetic pinning: every sound is specified outright rather than left to modern English habits. So æ is the vowel of 'cat' and a the open back vowel of 'father'; short and long vowels stay apart; ea and eo are sounded as two-part diphthongs; sc is 'sh', cg the 'j' of 'edge', hw a breathy w; h after a vowel is the rasp of German 'ach' or 'ich'; and doubled consonants are held long. The limits: the voice has no throaty g (dagas, lagu), so it says a plain g; long ǣ, long ȳ and long ēa are heard short; compounds are not split, so a sound at the seam of a compound is occasionally voiced where it should not be; and unstressed vowels keep their full quality. The reading is a model of one scholarly convention, as much a reconstruction as the text. Translations made fresh from the original.
about: Beowulf survives in a single manuscript, the Nowell Codex, which was scorched in a library fire in 1731; its edges have crumbled away, and some readings survive only in two transcripts made in 1787. What you read here is a reconstruction — Klaeber's edition of 1922 — and parts of it are educated guesswork: [brackets] mark letters editors added, (parentheses) mark letters restored where the manuscript is damaged or lost, and a few words are best guesses whose exact meaning no one knows. The notes say so where it matters. Line numbers are Klaeber's, the standard way of citing the poem.

sentences.l: He saw then among the war-gear a victory-blessed blade, an old sword, ettinish, doughty in its edges, the honour of warriors;
sentences.i: Then among the armour he saw a sword blessed with victory, an old blade made by giants, strong in its edges, a glory to warriors;
sentences.n: The subject of ‘Geseah’ (‘saw’) is unstated: it is Beowulf, just risen to his feet at the end of the last fitt. ‘on searwum’ is a dative plural, ‘among the war-gear’ (‘searu’, ‘armour, equipment’), so the sword is among the arms kept in her hall; at 249 the same phrase is ‘in war-gear’, of a man in his armour, and it could describe Beowulf here, but ‘among’ suits a sword he catches sight of. The accusatives ‘bil’, ‘ealdsweord’ and ‘wigena weorðmynd’ all name the one object. ‘sigeēadig’ is ‘victory-blessed’ (‘sige’ ‘victory’, ‘ēadig’ ‘blessed, prosperous’). ‘eotenisc’ is the adjective of ‘eoten’, the ettins of line 112, so ‘made by or belonging to giants’. ‘ecgum þȳhtig’ is ‘strong in edges’, ‘ecgum’ a dative plural of respect. ‘wigena’ is the genitive plural of ‘wiga’, ‘warrior’, and ‘weorðmynd’ is ‘honour, glory’: the sword is a glory of warriors. The apparatus records editors who print ‘eald sweord’ as two words.

sentences.t:
þæt [wæs] wǣpna cyst, —
būton hit wæs māre ðonne ǣnig mon ōðer
tō beadulāce ætberan meahte,
gōd ond geatolīc, gīganta geweorc.
sentences.l: that was the choicest of weapons — except that it was greater than any other man could carry to battle-play — good and splendid, the work of giants.
sentences.i: It was the finest of weapons, only it was bigger than any other man could have carried into the play of battle: a good and splendid thing, the work of giants.
sentences.n: ‘þæt [wæs] wǣpna cyst’ is ‘that was the choice of weapons’, ‘wǣpna’ a genitive plural with ‘cyst’, as in ‘īrena cyst’ at 673. The verb ‘wæs’ is not in the manuscript: Kemble supplied it (Grundtvig had proposed it with a query), and Klaeber prints it in brackets. ‘būton hit wæs māre’ is ‘except that it was greater’, and ‘ðonne ǣnig mon ōðer … ætberan meahte’ ‘than any other man could carry’, ‘ætberan’ ‘bear to, carry’. ‘beadulāc’ is ‘battle-play’ (‘beadu’ ‘battle’ and ‘lāc’ ‘play’, a word that also means ‘gift’), like ‘heaðolāc’ at 584. ‘geatolīc’ is ‘splendid, well-equipped’. ‘gīganta geweorc’ is ‘work of giants’: ‘gīgant’ is the Latin word, used for the giants who fought against God at 113. The dash after ‘cyst’ is Klaeber’s.

sentences.t:
Hē gefēng þā fetelhilt, freca Scyldinga
hrēoh ond heorogrim, hringmǣl gebrægd
aldres orwēna, yrringa slōh,
þæt hire wið halse heard grāpode,
bānhringas bræc;
sentences.l: He seized then the belt-hilt, the bold one of the Scyldings, fierce and sword-grim, drew the ring-marked blade, despairing of life, struck angrily, so that the hard one gripped her against the neck, broke the bone-rings;
sentences.i: The Scyldings’ champion, fierce and grim, seized the belted hilt and drew the patterned sword; with no hope left of life he struck in fury, so that the hard blade caught her on the neck and broke the rings of bone;
sentences.n: The subject ‘Hē’ is restated by ‘freca Scyldinga’, ‘the bold one of the Scyldings’ (‘freca’ ‘bold man, warrior’, as in ‘scyldfreca’ at 1033). Beowulf is a Geat, and the poem does not say why he is called a warrior of the Scyldings here; I take it as ‘fighting in the Danes’ cause’, which is a guess. ‘fetelhilt’ is ‘belt-hilt’, ‘fetel’ being a sword-belt or the ring that holds one. ‘heorogrim’ is ‘sword-grim’ or ‘fiercely grim’, with ‘heoro-’ perhaps only an intensifier, the same doubt as with ‘heorogīfre’ at 1498. ‘hringmǣl’ is ‘ring-marked’, the patterned sword, as at 1521, and ‘gebrægd’ the past of ‘gebregdan’, ‘draw’. ‘aldres orwēna’ is ‘hopeless of life’, ‘orwēna’ taking the genitive ‘aldres’. ‘yrringa’ is the adverb ‘angrily’. In the result clause ‘heard’ is the subject, ‘the hard one’, the sword; ‘hire wið halse’ is ‘against her neck’, ‘hire’ a dative, and ‘grāpode’ ‘gripped, seized’. ‘bānhringas’ is ‘bone-rings’, the joints of the spine, the object of ‘bræc’, ‘broke’. The apparatus notes that a new manuscript leaf (fol. 164b) begins with ‘slōh’, and gives the word on the authority of the two Thorkelin transcripts (A and B).

sentences.t:
bil eal ðurhwōd
fǣgne flǣschoman;
sentences.l: the blade went wholly through the doomed flesh-covering;
sentences.i: the sword passed clean through her doomed body;
sentences.n: ‘ðurhwōd’ is the past of ‘ðurhwadan’, ‘go through, pierce’ (‘wadan’ is ‘wade, go’), with ‘bil’ the subject and ‘eal’ the adverb ‘entirely’. ‘flǣschoma’ is ‘flesh-covering’ (‘flǣsc’ ‘flesh’ and ‘homa’ ‘covering’, the word in ‘fyrdhom’ at 1504), a kenning for the body. ‘fǣgne’ is the accusative of ‘fǣge’, ‘doomed to die’, the word used at 1527 of the doomed men whose war-gear Hrunting had cut.

sentences.t:
hēo on flet gecrong,
sweord wæs swātig, secg weorce gefeh.
sentences.l: she sank to the floor, the sword was sweaty, the man rejoiced in the work.
sentences.i: She fell dead to the floor; the sword was wet with blood, and the man was glad of his work.
sentences.n: ‘gecrong’ is the past of ‘gecringan’, ‘fall, fall dead’, and ‘on flet’ is ‘onto the floor’, as at 1540. ‘swātig’ is ‘sweaty’, from ‘swāt’, which means both sweat and blood (as in ‘heaþoswāt’, ‘battle-sweat’, at 1460); here it is blood. ‘gefeh’ is the past of ‘gefēon’, ‘rejoice’, with the dative ‘weorce’, ‘in the work, the deed’; ‘weorc’ can also mean ‘pain, toil’, but the man’s joy is in what he has done. Three short clauses, each with its own subject, close the fight.

sentences.t:
Līxte se lēoma, lēoht inne stōd,
efne swā of hefene hādre scīneð
rodores candel.
sentences.l: The beam gleamed, light stood within, even as from heaven brightly shines the sky’s candle.
sentences.i: The light flashed out and brightness filled the place, just as the candle of the sky shines clear from heaven.
sentences.n: ‘Līxte’ is the past of ‘līxan’, ‘shine, flash’, and ‘se lēoma’, ‘the beam, the gleam’, is its subject; ‘lēoht inne stōd’ is ‘light stood within’, ‘stōd’ used of a light that holds steady. Which light this is the text does not say: ‘se lēoma’, with the definite article, may be the ‘blācne lēoman’ seen at 1517, flaring up now, or a new light at the monster’s death; I leave it open. ‘efne swā’ is ‘even as’, ‘hādre’ the adverb ‘brightly, clearly’, and ‘rodores candel’ ‘the sky’s candle’, a kenning for the sun (‘rodor’ ‘sky, heaven’, as in ‘rodera Rǣdend’ at 1555).

sentences.t:
Hē æfter recede wlāt;
hwearf þā be wealle, wǣpen hafenade
heard be hiltum Higelāces ðegn
yrre ond anrǣd, —
sentences.l: He looked along the hall; turned then along the wall, raised the weapon, hard, by its hilts, Higelac’s thane, angry and resolute, —
sentences.i: He looked about the hall and moved along the wall; Higelac’s thane, angry and resolute, raised the hard weapon by its hilt —
sentences.n: ‘æfter recede’ is ‘along the hall’, ‘æfter’ with the dative meaning ‘through, along’; ‘wlāt’ is the past of ‘wlītan’, ‘look’. ‘hwearf’ is the past of ‘hweorfan’, ‘turn, go’, and ‘be wealle’ is ‘along the wall’. ‘hafenade’ is the past of ‘hafenian’, ‘raise, lift up’, with ‘wǣpen’ its object. ‘heard’ can agree with ‘wǣpen’ (neuter accusative, ‘the hard weapon’) or with ‘Higelāces ðegn’ (masculine nominative, ‘the hardy thane’); I give it to the weapon. ‘be hiltum’ is a dative plural, ‘by the hilts’, and the hilt is plural again at 1614 (‘þā hilt’). ‘Higelāces ðegn’, ‘Higelac’s thane’, the title of 194, is the subject, and ‘yrre ond anrǣd’ (‘angry and resolute’) describe him. Klaeber’s dash marks a turn in the sentence: the narrator now says why the sword is raised.

sentences.t:
næs sēo ecg fracod
hilderince, ac hē hraþe wolde
Grendle forgyldan gūðrǣsa fela
ðāra þe hē geworhte tō West-Denum
oftor micle ðonne on ǣnne sīð,
sentences.l: the edge was not worthless to the battle-man, but he quickly would repay Grendel for many war-rushes, of those that he had worked upon the West-Danes much oftener than on one occasion,
sentences.i: The edge was no useless thing to the warrior: he meant at once to pay Grendel back for the many onslaughts he had made on the West-Danes, far more often than one time,
sentences.n: ‘næs’ here is ‘ne wæs’, ‘was not’, and ‘fracod’ is ‘vile, worthless’: ‘the edge was not worthless to the warrior’, with ‘hilderince’ the dative (as at 1495). ‘forgyldan’ is ‘repay’, with the dative of the person, ‘Grendle’, and the accusative ‘gūðrǣsa fela’, ‘many war-rushes’ (‘gūðrǣs’ ‘battle-onset’, ‘fela’ with the genitive plural), for what is paid back. ‘ðāra þe hē geworhte’ is ‘of those which he wrought’, and ‘tō West-Denum’ ‘against the West-Danes’, the compass-name for the Danes as at 383. ‘oftor micle ðonne on ǣnne sīð’ is ‘much oftener than on one occasion’, ‘micle’ an instrumental, ‘by much’. Beowulf’s anger turns from the mother to the son, and the next lines name the first raid.

sentences.t:
þonne hē Hrōðgāres heorðgenēatas
slōh on sweofote, slǣpende frǣt
folces Denigea fȳftȳne men,
ond ōðer swylc ūt offerede,
lāðlicu lāc.
sentences.l: when he slew Hrothgar’s hearth-companions in their sleep, devoured, sleeping, fifteen men of the Danish people, and another such carried off outside, a loathsome offering.
sentences.i: when he killed Hrothgar’s hearth-companions as they slept, devoured fifteen men of the Danes in their sleep and carried as many more away, a hateful prize.
sentences.n: ‘þonne’ with the past ‘slōh’ is ‘when’, of a time now past. ‘heorðgenēatas’ is ‘hearth-companions’, as at 261. ‘on sweofote’ is ‘in sleep’ (‘swefot’, ‘sleep’), and ‘slǣpende’ a present participle, accusative plural, agreeing with ‘men’: he devoured them sleeping. ‘frǣt’ is the past of ‘fretan’, ‘devour, eat up’. ‘folces Denigea’ is ‘of the people of the Danes’. ‘ōðer swylc’ is ‘another such (number)’, and ‘offerede’ the past of ‘offerian’, ‘carry off’, with ‘ūt’ ‘out’. Fifteen eaten and fifteen carried off make the thirty thanes of Grendel’s first raid at 123. ‘lāðlicu lāc’ is ‘a loathsome gift’ (the ending of ‘lāðlicu’ fits a singular or a plural, ‘loathsome gifts’): ‘lāc’, the ‘play’ of ‘beadulāc’ at 1561, also means a gift or offering, so the carried-off dead are called, grimly, a present.

sentences.t:
Hē him þæs lēan forgeald,
rēþe cempa, tō ðæs þe hē on ræste geseah
gūðwērigne Grendel licgan,
aldorlēasne, swā him ǣr gescōd
hild æt Heorote.
sentences.l: He paid him the reward for that, the fierce champion, to the point that he saw Grendel lie on his resting-place, war-weary, lifeless, as battle at Heorot had harmed him before.
sentences.i: The fierce champion paid him what he had earned for that, to the point where he saw Grendel lying on his bed, worn out by war and lifeless, as the fight at Heorot had left him.
sentences.n: ‘Hē him þæs lēan forgeald’ is ‘he repaid him the reward for that’, ‘þæs’ a genitive ‘for that’ and ‘lēan’ the accusative ‘reward, requital’: the same half-line is said of God and the giants at 114. ‘rēþe cempa’, ‘the fierce champion’, Beowulf, stands in apposition to ‘Hē’. ‘tō ðæs þe’ is ‘to the point that’, or ‘to where’; the lexica allow both and I take the first, a guess. At 714 the same phrase was rendered ‘until’. ‘on ræste’ is ‘on his resting-place, bed’, the phrase used of the sleeping Danes at 122. ‘gūðwērigne’ is ‘war-weary’ and ‘aldorlēasne’ ‘lifeless’ (‘aldor’ ‘life’; the same compound means ‘lordless’ at 15, where ‘aldor’ is ‘lord’). Both are accusatives agreeing with ‘Grendel’, the subject of the infinitive ‘licgan’. ‘swā him ǣr gescōd hild æt Heorote’ is ‘as battle at Heorot had harmed him before’, ‘gescōd’ the past of ‘gesceþðan’ with the dative ‘him’. Grendel had gone home from Heorot to die (850–851).

sentences.t:
Hrā wīde sprong,
syþðan hē æfter dēaðe drepe þrōwade,
heorosweng heardne, ond hine þā hēafde becearf.
sentences.l: The corpse sprang wide, when he after death suffered a blow, a hard sword-swing, and he then cut him off from his head.
sentences.i: The corpse leapt far as it took the stroke after death, a hard blow of the sword, and then he cut off Grendel’s head.
sentences.n: ‘Hrā’ is ‘corpse’, neuter, and ‘sprong’ the past of ‘springan’, ‘spring, leap’: the dead body jerked far under the blow. In ‘syþðan hē … drepe þrōwade’ the ‘hē’ is Grendel, ‘þrōwade’ the past of ‘þrōwian’, ‘suffer’, and ‘drepe’ the accusative of ‘drepe’, ‘blow, stroke’, with ‘heorosweng heardne’ (‘a hard sword-swing’) in apposition; here ‘heoro-’ plainly means ‘sword’. In the last clause ‘hine’ is Grendel and the unstated subject Beowulf: ‘becearf’ is the past of ‘beceorfan’, ‘cut off, deprive of’, with the accusative of the person and the dative ‘hēafde’ of what is cut away, so ‘cut him off from his head’. In Heorot Beowulf took Grendel’s arm and shoulder (833–835); now he takes the head.

sentences.t:
Sōna þæt gesāwon snottre ceorlas,
þā ðe mid Hrōðgāre on holm wliton,
þæt wæs ȳðgeblond eal gemenged,
brim blōde fāh.
sentences.l: Soon that saw the wise men, those who with Hrothgar were looking on the water, that the wave-blending was all stirred up, the sea stained with blood.
sentences.i: Soon the wise men who were watching the water with Hrothgar saw the surging waves all churned up, the sea stained with blood.
sentences.n: ‘þæt’ is the object of ‘gesāwon’, ‘saw’, looking forward to the second ‘þæt’ clause, which says what they saw. ‘snottre ceorlas’ is ‘the wise men’: ‘ceorl’ is a man, here one of the king’s older counsellors. ‘þā ðe … on holm wliton’ is ‘those who looked on the water’, ‘wliton’ the plural past of ‘wlītan’, the verb of 1572. ‘ȳðgeblond’ is ‘wave-blending’, the surging water, as at 1373; ‘gemenged’ is the past participle of ‘mengan’, ‘mix, stir up’. ‘brim blōde fāh’ is ‘the sea stained with blood’, ‘fāh’ ‘coloured, stained’ and ‘blōde’ a dative. The apparatus notes that a new manuscript leaf (fol. 165a) begins at ‘ceorlas’. The scene moves from the hall under the water to the men on the shore above.

sentences.t:
Blondenfeaxe,
gomele ymb gōdne ongeador sprǣcon,
þæt hig þæs æðelinges eft ne wēndon,
þæt hē sigehrēðig sēcean cōme
mǣrne þēoden;
sentences.l: The blended-haired ones, the old ones, spoke together about the good one, that they did not expect of the atheling again that he, victory-glorious, would come to seek the famed lord;
sentences.i: The grey-haired old men spoke together about the good man, saying they did not expect the prince to come back in triumph to seek out their famous lord;
sentences.n: ‘Blondenfeaxe’ is ‘mixed-haired’ (‘blonden’, the past participle of ‘blandan’, ‘mix’, with ‘feax’ ‘hair’), so ‘grizzled, grey-haired’; with ‘gomele’, ‘the old ones’, it is the subject of ‘sprǣcon’, ‘spoke’. ‘ymb gōdne’ is ‘about the good one’, Beowulf, and ‘ongeador’ ‘together’. ‘wēndon’ is the past of ‘wēnan’, ‘expect’, which takes the genitive ‘þæs æðelinges’: ‘they did not expect of the prince’, and the clause ‘þæt hē … cōme’ says what. ‘cōme’ is a past subjunctive, and ‘sēcean’ an infinitive of purpose after it, ‘come to seek’. ‘sigehrēðig’ is ‘victory-glorious, triumphant’. ‘mǣrne þēoden’, ‘the famed lord’, is Hrothgar, the object of ‘sēcean’, as at 201.

sentences.t:
þā ðæs monige gewearð,
þæt hine sēo brimwylf ābroten hæfde.
sentences.l: then about that many came to agree, that the sea-she-wolf had destroyed him.
sentences.i: Many of them were now agreed that the she-wolf of the sea had killed him.
sentences.n: ‘þā ðæs monige gewearð’ is impersonal: ‘geweorðan’ with an accusative of the persons (‘monige’, ‘many’) and a genitive of the matter (‘ðæs’, ‘about that’) means ‘it came to be agreed by them’, so ‘then many came to agree on that’. The construction is rare and I follow the lexica, with some doubt. The ‘þæt’ clause says what they agreed on. ‘sēo brimwylf’ is the house ‘sea-she-wolf’, as at 1506. ‘ābroten’ is the past participle of ‘ābrēotan’, ‘destroy, kill’: the manuscript has ‘abreoten’, and Kemble’s correction ‘ābroten’ is what Klaeber prints, with the changed ‘o’ in italic. The watchers are wrong: the blood in the water is the monsters’.

sentences.t: Ðā cōm nōn dæges.
sentences.l: Then came the ninth hour of the day.
sentences.i: Then the ninth hour of the day came on.
sentences.n: ‘nōn’ is the Latin ‘nona (hora)’, the ninth hour of the day counted from sunrise, about three in the afternoon, a church hour borrowed into English and the source of ‘noon’. ‘dæges’ is a genitive, ‘of the day’. The poem keeps count of the time of the dive: at 1495 ‘a while of day’ passed before Beowulf reached the bottom.

sentences.t:
Næs ofgēafon
hwate Scyldingas; gewāt him hām þonon
goldwine gumena.
sentences.l: The headland the bold Scyldings abandoned; the gold-friend of men took himself home from there.
sentences.i: The bold Scyldings left the headland, and the gold-friend of men went home from there.
sentences.n: ‘Næs’ is the noun ‘ness, headland’, the accusative object of ‘ofgēafon’, ‘gave up, left’ (‘ofgiefan’), and not ‘ne wæs’ as at 1575; the plural verb and the sense decide it. ‘hwate Scyldingas’ is ‘the bold Scyldings’. ‘gewāt him’ is ‘took himself off’, ‘gewītan’ with the reflexive dative ‘him’, and ‘hām þonon’ ‘home from there’. ‘goldwine gumena’ is ‘gold-friend of men’, the kenning for a generous king used at 1171 and 1476, here Hrothgar.

sentences.t:
Gistas sētan
mōdes sēoce ond on mere staredon;
wīston ond ne wēndon, þæt hīe heora winedrihten
selfne gesāwon. —
sentences.l: The guests sat sick of mind and stared on the mere; they wished and did not expect that they would see their friend-lord himself. —
sentences.i: The strangers sat on, sick at heart, and stared at the mere; they wished, but did not expect, to see their dear lord himself again. —
sentences.n: ‘Gistas’ is ‘guests, strangers’, here the Geats who came with Beowulf. ‘sētan’ is ‘sat’: the manuscript has ‘secan’ (‘seek’), which gives no sense with ‘mōdes sēoce’; Grundtvig proposed ‘sǣton’ and Grein ‘sētan’, which Klaeber prints with the changed ‘t’ in italic. ‘mōdes sēoce’ is ‘sick of mind’, ‘mōdes’ a genitive of respect. ‘staredon’ is ‘stared’, and ‘on mere’ ‘at the mere’. Klaeber’s long ‘ī’ in ‘wīston’ marks it as a past of ‘wȳscan’, ‘wish’, without its ‘c’; Kemble prints ‘wȳs[c]ton’, and Thorpe and Grundtvig ‘wīs[c]ton’, to make that plain. ‘wiston’ with a short vowel, ‘knew’, would clash with ‘ne wēndon’, ‘did not expect’; I follow Klaeber, but the reading is a guess. ‘winedrihten’ is ‘friend-lord’, as at 862, and ‘selfne’ ‘himself’, that is, alive. The dash after the full stop is Klaeber’s.

sentences.l: Then that sword began, after the battle-sweat, in battle-icicles, the war-blade, to wane;
sentences.i: Then the sword, that war-blade, began to waste away in icicles of battle from the blood of battle;
sentences.n: ‘ongan … wanian’ is ‘began to wane, dwindle’, with ‘þæt sweord’ and ‘wīgbil’ (‘war-blade’) the double subject, set apart by the phrase between them. ‘æfter heaþoswāte’ is ‘after, because of the battle-sweat’, the house ‘battle-sweat’ for the blood of the fight, as at 1460. ‘hildegicelum’ is a dative plural, ‘in battle-icicles’ (‘hild’ ‘battle’ and ‘gicel’ ‘icicle’, the second half of the English word ‘icicle’): the blade runs off in drops, like ice thawing. The lexica record the compound only here.

sentences.t:
þæt wæs wundra sum,
þæt hit eal gemealt īse gelīcost,
ðonne forstes bend Fæder onlǣteð,
onwindeð wǣlrāpas, sē geweald hafað
sǣla ond mǣla; þæt is sōð Metod.
sentences.l: that was a certain one of wonders, that it all melted most like ice, when the Father loosens the frost’s bond, unwinds the pool-ropes, he who has power over seasons and times; that is the true Measurer.
sentences.i: That was a marvel, that it melted away entirely, most like ice when the Father loosens the bonds of frost and unwinds the fetters of the water, he who has power over seasons and times; he is the true Lord.
sentences.n: ‘wundra sum’ is ‘one of wonders’, a partitive genitive, so ‘a marvel’, and the ‘þæt’ clause says what it was. ‘gemealt’ is the past of ‘gemeltan’, ‘melt’, and ‘īse gelīcost’ ‘most like ice’, the superlative of ‘gelīc’ with the dative ‘īse’. In the ‘ðonne’ clause ‘Fæder’ is the subject, the house ‘Father’ for God, and ‘forstes bend’ (‘the frost’s bond’) the object of ‘onlǣteð’, ‘lets loose’. ‘onwindeð’ is ‘unwinds’, and ‘wǣlrāpas’ is a compound the lexica record only here: I read it as ‘pool-ropes’ (‘wǣl’, with a long vowel, ‘deep water, pool’, and ‘rāp’ ‘rope’), the ice that binds the water, which is a guess; several editors change it to ‘wǣgrāpas’, ‘wave-ropes’. ‘sē geweald hafað sǣla ond mǣla’ is ‘who has power over seasons and times’, ‘geweald’ with the genitive (‘sǣl’ ‘season, fit time’, ‘mǣl’ ‘time, occasion’). ‘sōð Metod’ is ‘the true Measurer’, ‘Metod’ the old name of God met first at 110. The melting sword leads the narrator to the God who governs the seasons.

sentences.t:
Ne nōm hē in þǣm wīcum, Weder-Gēata lēod,
māðmǣhta mā, þēh hē þǣr monige geseah,
būton þone hafelan ond þā hilt somod
since fāge;
sentences.l: He did not take in those dwellings, the Weder-Geats’ man, more of treasure-possessions, though he saw many there, except the head and the hilt together, adorned with treasure;
sentences.i: The Geat took no more of the treasures in that dwelling, though he saw many there, only the head, and with it the hilt, bright with treasure;
sentences.n: ‘nōm’ is a past of ‘niman’, ‘take’ (the commoner form is ‘nam’), and ‘Weder-Gēata lēod’ is the house ‘Weder-Geats’ man’, as at 1492, the subject. ‘in þǣm wīcum’ is a dative plural, ‘in those dwellings’, the plural used of one home. ‘māðmǣhta mā’ is ‘more of treasure-possessions’, ‘mā’ taking the genitive plural of ‘māðmǣht’ (‘māðm’ ‘treasure’ and ‘ǣht’ ‘possession’). ‘þēh’ is a form of ‘þēah’, ‘though’. ‘būton’ is ‘except’, and its objects are ‘þone hafelan’, ‘the head’ (Grendel’s), and ‘þā hilt’, ‘the hilt’, with a plural article; ‘somod’ is ‘together, as well’. ‘since fāge’ is ‘adorned with treasure’, ‘fāh’ ‘coloured, decorated’ (the word that meant ‘stained’ at 1594) with the dative ‘since’, and it describes the hilt.

sentences.t:
sweord ǣr gemealt,
forbarn brōdenmǣl; wæs þæt blōd tō þæs hāt,
ættren ellorgǣst, sē þǣr inne swealt.
sentences.l: the sword had already melted, the braided-marked blade burned up; that blood was so hot, the elsewhere-ghost poisonous, who died there within.
sentences.i: The sword had already melted, the patterned blade burnt away, so hot was that blood, so poisonous the spirit from elsewhere who had died in there.
sentences.n: ‘ǣr gemealt’ is ‘had melted before’, the simple past with ‘ǣr’ doing the work of a pluperfect. ‘forbarn’ is the past of ‘forbeornan’, ‘burn up’, and ‘brōdenmǣl’ (‘braided-marked’: ‘brōden’ ‘woven, braided’ and ‘mǣl’ ‘mark’) is another name for a patterned blade, like ‘hringmǣl’ at 1564 and ‘wundenmǣl’ at 1531. ‘tō þæs hāt’ is ‘so hot’ (‘tō þæs’, ‘to that degree’). ‘ættren ellorgǣst’ has no verb of its own: I read it as ‘(and) the elsewhere-ghost (was so) poisonous’, sharing ‘wæs … tō þæs’, which is the plainest construction but still a guess. ‘ellorgǣst’ is ‘elsewhere-ghost’, a spirit from elsewhere (‘ellor’ ‘elsewhere’), as in the plural ‘ellorgǣstas’ at 1349; the apparatus notes that in the manuscript ‘ellor’ was altered from ‘ellen’. ‘sē þǣr inne swealt’ is ‘who died in there’, ‘swealt’ the past of ‘sweltan’. Which monster is meant the text does not say: the mother was killed in that hall, but the sword was last used on Grendel’s body. The apparatus also marks a new manuscript leaf (fol. 165b) at ‘tō’, read from the two Thorkelin transcripts.

sentences.t:
Sōna wæs on sunde sē þe ǣr æt sæcce gebād
wīghryre wrāðra, wæter ūp þurhdēaf;
sentences.l: Soon he was swimming, he who before at the strife had lived through the war-fall of the hostile ones; he dived up through the water;
sentences.i: Soon the man who had lived through the fall of his foes in the fight was swimming, and dived up through the water;
sentences.n: ‘on sunde’ is ‘in swimming, afloat’ (‘sund’, ‘swimming, sea’). The subject is the relative ‘sē þe … gebād’, ‘he who had lived to see’, ‘gebād’ the past of ‘gebīdan’, ‘wait for, live through’, with the object ‘wīghryre wrāðra’, ‘the war-fall of the hostile ones’ (‘wīghryre’ ‘fall in battle’, ‘wrāðra’ the genitive plural of ‘wrāð’, ‘hostile’), that is, the death of the two monsters. The apparatus records editors who read ‘wīggryre’, ‘war-terror’. ‘þurhdēaf’ is the past of ‘þurhdūfan’, ‘dive through’, with ‘wæter’ its object and ‘ūp’ ‘upward’.

sentences.t:
wǣron ȳðgebland eal gefǣlsod,
ēacne eardas, þā se ellorgāst
oflēt līfdagas ond þās lǣnan gesceaft.
sentences.l: the wave-blendings were all cleansed, the vast regions, when the elsewhere-ghost left its life-days and this loaned creation.
sentences.i: The surging waters were all cleansed, the wide expanses, now that the spirit from elsewhere had given up the days of its life and this passing world.
sentences.n: ‘wǣron … gefǣlsod’ is a plural passive, ‘were cleansed’, so ‘ȳðgebland’ (‘wave-blending’, spelled here with ‘a’ where 1593 has ‘ȳðgeblond’) is plural, with ‘ēacne eardas’ (‘the vast regions’, ‘ēacen’ ‘enlarged, great’) in apposition. ‘gefǣlsian’ is the verb of the cleansing of Heorot at 825, and the simple ‘fǣlsian’ at 432. ‘þā’ is ‘when’; ‘oflēt’ is the past of ‘oflǣtan’, ‘leave, give up’, with two objects, ‘līfdagas’ (‘life-days’) and ‘þās lǣnan gesceaft’ (‘this loaned creation’). ‘lǣne’ is ‘lent, transitory’: the world is held on loan. ‘ellorgāst’ is ‘ellorgǣst’ of 1617 with the other vowel, the form used at 807.

sentences.t:
Cōm þā tō lande lidmanna helm
swīðmōd swymman; sǣlāce gefeah,
mægenbyrþenne þāra þe hē him mid hæfde.
sentences.l: Came then to land the helm of seafarers, strong-minded, swimming; he rejoiced in the sea-gift, the mighty burden of those which he had with him.
sentences.i: Then the sailors’ protector came swimming to land, stout of heart; he was glad of his booty from the sea, the great burden of the things he had with him.
sentences.n: ‘Cōm … swymman’ is ‘came swimming’, a verb of motion with an infinitive. ‘lidmanna helm’ is ‘the helm of the seafarers’ (‘lidman’ ‘seafarer’, from ‘lid’ ‘ship’), ‘helm’ in its sense ‘protector’: Beowulf as leader of the men who sailed with him. ‘swīðmōd’ is ‘strong-minded’. ‘gefeah’ is the past of ‘gefēon’, ‘rejoice’, here with the dative ‘sǣlāce’, ‘sea-gift, booty from the sea’ (‘lāc’ as at 1584), and ‘mægenbyrþenne’, ‘mighty burden’, stands in apposition. ‘þāra þe hē him mid hæfde’ is ‘of those which he had with him’: the genitive plural ‘þāra’ hangs loosely on a singular noun, and the apparatus records an editor who drops it, others who read the singular ‘þǣre’, and others who make the noun a genitive plural, ‘sǣlāca’. The burden is the head and the hilt.

sentences.t:
Ēodon him þā tōgēanes, Gode þancodon,
ðrȳðlīc þegna hēap, þēodnes gefēgon,
þæs þe hī hyne gesundne gesēon mōston.
sentences.l: Went then toward him, gave thanks to God, the mighty band of thanes, rejoiced in their prince, because they might see him sound.
sentences.i: The splendid band of thanes went out to meet him and thanked God, glad of their lord, because they were granted the sight of him safe and sound.
sentences.n: The plural verbs ‘Ēodon’ (‘went’), ‘þancodon’ (‘thanked’) and ‘gefēgon’ (‘rejoiced’) all have the subject ‘ðrȳðlīc þegna hēap’, ‘the mighty band of thanes’, a singular noun for a company taking a plural verb. ‘him … tōgēanes’ is ‘towards him’. ‘Gode þancodon’, with the dative ‘Gode’, is the formula of 625 and 1397 in the plural. ‘gefēgon’ takes the genitive ‘þēodnes’, ‘in the prince’. ‘þæs þe’ is ‘because’, ‘mōston’ ‘were allowed, could’, and ‘gesundne’ ‘sound, unharmed’, an accusative agreeing with ‘hyne’.

sentences.t:
Ðā wæs of þǣm hrōran helm ond byrne
lungre ālȳsed.
sentences.l: Then from the vigorous one helm and byrnie were quickly loosed.
sentences.i: Then helmet and mail-shirt were quickly unfastened from the strong man.
sentences.n: The verb ‘wæs … ālȳsed’ is singular with two subjects, ‘helm ond byrne’, as Old English often allows. ‘ālȳsed’ is the past participle of ‘ālȳsan’, ‘loosen, release’, and ‘lungre’ is ‘quickly’. ‘of þǣm hrōran’ is ‘from the vigorous one’, ‘hrōran’ the weak form of ‘hrōr’, ‘strong, active’, used as a noun for Beowulf.

sentences.t:
Lagu drūsade,
wæter under wolcnum, wældrēore fāg.
sentences.l: The lake grew still, the water under the clouds, stained with slaughter-gore.
sentences.i: The lake lay quiet, the water under the clouds, stained with the blood of slaughter.
sentences.n: ‘Lagu’ is ‘water, lake, sea’, and ‘drūsade’ is the past of ‘drūsian’, which the lexica give as ‘become sluggish, subside’; I take it as ‘grew still’, a guess from very little evidence. ‘wæter under wolcnum’ (‘water under the clouds’) restates the subject. ‘wældrēore fāg’ is ‘stained with slaughter-gore’, from ‘wæl’ ‘slaughter’ and ‘drēor’ ‘gore, blood’, with ‘fāg’ a spelling of ‘fāh’.

sentences.l: They went forth from there in foot-tracks, glad in spirits, measured the earth-way, the known street;
sentences.i: They set out from there on foot, glad at heart, and paced the way over the land, the familiar road;
sentences.n: ‘Fērdon’ is the plural past of ‘fēran’, ‘go, travel’, and the subject, the Geats, is unstated. ‘fēþelāstum’ is a dative plural, ‘with foot-tracks’, so ‘on foot’. ‘ferhþum fægne’ is ‘glad in their spirits’, ‘fægne’ the plural of ‘fægen’, ‘glad’, with a short ‘æ’; it is a different word from ‘fǣgne’, ‘doomed’, at 1568. ‘mǣton’ is the past plural of ‘metan’, ‘measure’, so ‘measured out, travelled’, with ‘foldweg’ (‘earth-way’) and ‘cūþe strǣte’ (‘the known road’) as objects: they go back by the way they came.

sentences.t:
cyningbalde men
from þǣm holmclife hafelan bǣron
earfoðlīce heora ǣghwæþrum
felamōdigra;
sentences.l: the king-bold men bore the head from the sea-cliff with difficulty for each of them, of the very brave ones;
sentences.i: Those royally brave men carried the head from the cliff above the water, and it was hard work for each of them, bold as they were;
sentences.n: ‘cyningbalde’ is ‘king-bold’, a compound the lexica record only here, and its meaning is a guess: I take it as ‘bold as kings, royally brave’. The apparatus records editors who read ‘cynebalde’, with much the same sense, and Bugge’s ‘cyningholde’, ‘loyal to the king’. ‘holmclif’ is the ‘sea-cliff’ above the mere, and ‘hafelan bǣron’ is ‘carried the head’. ‘earfoðlīce’ is ‘with difficulty’, and ‘heora ǣghwæþrum felamōdigra’ is a dative of the person affected, ‘for each of them, of the very brave’: ‘ǣghwæþer’ properly means ‘each of two’, which sits oddly with four bearers, and ‘felamōdigra’ is a genitive plural, ‘of the much-spirited’.

sentences.t:
fēower scoldon
on þǣm wælstenge weorcum geferian
tō þǣm goldsele Grendles hēafod, —
sentences.l: four had to carry, on the slaughter-pole, with toils, to the gold-hall Grendel’s head, —
sentences.i: it took four of them to carry Grendel’s head on a pole to the gold-hall, with great labour —
sentences.n: ‘fēower scoldon … geferian’ is ‘four had to carry’, ‘scoldon’ the past of ‘sculan’ and ‘geferian’ ‘carry, convey’, with ‘Grendles hēafod’ the object. ‘wælsteng’ is ‘slaughter-pole’ (‘wæl’ ‘slaughter’ and ‘steng’ ‘pole, stake’), a pole for carrying the head; the lexica record the word only here, and whether it is a spear-shaft or a pole cut for the purpose the text does not say. ‘weorcum’ is a dative plural, ‘with toils, laboriously’. ‘goldsele’ is ‘gold-hall’, Heorot. The size of the head matches the size of the giants’ sword. The dash is Klaeber’s.

sentences.l: until suddenly to the hall came, bold, army-keen, fourteen of the Geats walking;
sentences.i: until suddenly fourteen Geats, bold and eager for war, came marching to the hall;
sentences.n: ‘oþ ðæt’ is ‘until’, and ‘semninga’ ‘suddenly, at once’. ‘cōmon … gongan’ is ‘came walking’, the motion verb with an infinitive, as at 1624. ‘frome fyrdhwate’ is ‘bold, war-keen’ (‘from’ ‘bold, active’; ‘fyrd’ ‘army, campaign’ and ‘hwæt’ ‘keen’), and ‘fēowertȳne Gēata’ is ‘fourteen of the Geats’, a partitive genitive. The apparatus marks a new manuscript leaf (fol. 166a) at ‘semninga’.

sentences.t:
gumdryhten mid
mōdig on gemonge meodowongas træd.
sentences.l: the lord of men with them, proud in the throng, trod the mead-plains.
sentences.i: and their lord, high-hearted among the company, walked with them over the meadows about the mead-hall.
sentences.n: ‘mid’ stands at the end of the half-line as an adverb, ‘along, with them’. ‘gumdryhten’ is ‘lord of men’ (‘guma’ ‘man’ and ‘dryhten’ ‘lord’), Beowulf as leader of his band, and ‘mōdig on gemonge’ ‘high-spirited in the throng’. ‘træd’ is the past of ‘tredan’, ‘tread’, and ‘meodowongas’ ‘mead-plains’, the fields around the hall where mead is drunk.

sentences.t:
Ðā cōm in gân ealdor ðegna,
dǣdcēne mon dōme gewurþad,
hæle hildedēor, Hrōðgār grētan.
sentences.l: Then came in walking the chief of thanes, the deed-bold man honoured with glory, the battle-brave hero, to greet Hrothgar.
sentences.i: Then the chief of the thanes came walking in, a man bold in deeds and honoured with renown, a hero brave in battle, to greet Hrothgar.
sentences.n: ‘cōm in gân’ is ‘came in walking’, with ‘gân’ the infinitive of ‘gān’, ‘go’; the circumflex is Klaeber’s mark for a contracted vowel, and the apparatus refers back to the same form at 386. ‘ealdor ðegna’ is ‘chief of thanes’ (‘ealdor’ ‘elder, chief’), Beowulf, with three more nominatives in apposition: ‘dǣdcēne mon’ (‘deed-bold man’), ‘dōme gewurþad’ (‘honoured with glory’, ‘gewurþad’ the past participle of ‘gewurþian’), and ‘hæle hildedēor’ (‘battle-brave hero’, ‘hæle’ ‘man, hero’; ‘hildedēor’ as at 312). ‘Hrōðgār grētan’ is the infinitive of purpose, ‘to greet Hrothgar’.

sentences.t:
Þā wæs be feaxe on flet boren
Grendles hēafod, þǣr guman druncon,
egeslīc for eorlum ond þǣre idese mid,
wlitesēon wrǣtlīc; weras on sāwon.
sentences.l: Then was borne by the hair onto the floor Grendel’s head, where men drank, terrible before the earls and the lady with them, a wondrous spectacle; the men looked on.
sentences.i: Then Grendel’s head was carried by the hair onto the floor where the men were drinking, a terrible thing before the warriors and the lady among them, a wondrous sight; the men gazed at it.
sentences.n: ‘wæs … boren’ is a passive, ‘was carried’, with ‘Grendles hēafod’ the subject. ‘be feaxe’ is ‘by the hair’, ‘feax’ as in ‘blondenfeaxe’ at 1594, and ‘on flet’ ‘onto the floor’ of the hall. ‘þǣr guman druncon’ is ‘where men were drinking’. ‘egeslīc’ (‘terrible’) and ‘wlitesēon wrǣtlīc’ (‘a wondrous sight’) describe the head; ‘wlitesēon’ is ‘sight to look at’ (‘wlite’ ‘look, beauty’ and ‘sēon’ ‘sight’). ‘for eorlum ond þǣre idese mid’ is ‘before the earls and the lady with them’, ‘idese’ the dative of ‘ides’, ‘woman, lady’, and ‘mid’ an adverb; the lady is not named, and the queen is the likeliest. The last half-line follows Sievers’ punctuation, as the apparatus says: ‘weras on sāwon’ is ‘the men looked on’, ‘on’ an adverb with ‘sāwon’. Earlier editors print ‘onsāwon’, ‘looked at’, with ‘wlitesēon’ as its object, ‘the men looked on the wondrous sight’; the sense is close either way.
